payload.author: shahabhilash
payload.body:
### Problem or motivation

 The current weekly digest service (weeklyDigestService.js) queues separate BullMQ jobs for every single user. Each job makes a separate prompt request to the Gemini API (gemini-2.5-flash) via generateWeeklyInsights(). For a large user base (e.g., thousands of active users), this creates:

Severe API Rate Limiting (429 Errors): Exceeds the RPM limits of free and paid Gemini API keys when processing concurrent queue jobs.
High Token Overhead & Cost: Generating market trends and generic career tips for users with identical roles (e.g., "Software Engineer") results in highly redundant prompts and completion costs.
Execution Delay: Processing users individually takes hours.

### Proposed solution

Refactor the weekly digest pipeline to run in two stages:

Batch/Generate & Cache (Stage 1):
Query all unique jobRoles for active users.
Make a single Gemini call per unique jobRole to generate the weekly market trends, generic career tips, and recommended skills.
Cache this template content in Redis or a temporary MongoDB collection keyed by role and week (e.g., digest:insights:${role}:${weekKey}).
Distribute & Compile (Stage 2):
The BullMQ worker for each user retrieves the user's jobRole and fetches the pre-generated insights template from the cache.
Append user-specific data (like their TrackedJobs list, which is deterministic and does not require AI processing) to the email template.
Compile and send the final HTML email.
This reduces Gemini API consumption from $N$ (number of users) to $M$ (number of unique job roles), guaranteeing stability, keeping costs low, and speeding up delivery.

### Alternatives considered

Staggering Queue Jobs: We currently attempt this using a 500ms delay between jobs (delay: index * 500). However, this does not scale. For 10,000 users, the last user will be delayed by over 80 minutes, and concurrency will still trigger 429 rate limit exceptions if workers process jobs faster than the API rate limit resets.
Using a local model / Ollama: Too slow and resource-heavy for standard cloud/VPS host instances.


### Additional context

Key code files affected:

backend/src/services/weeklyDigestService.js

backend/src/templates/emails/weekly-digest.html
 (if any template updates are needed)

### Area

Backend

payload.body:
### What happened?

The scheduled job alert system (triggered via Cron/BullMQ) fetches job listings from external APIs and local scrapers, saves them to the Mongoose database, and emails them to the user. However, the system does not check the NotificationLog to filter out job listings that have already been sent to that user in previous runs. This results in the user receiving the exact same job listings in their email inbox every time the scheduler runs.

### Steps to reproduce

Create a user account and set up a Job Alert (e.g. for "Software Engineer" in "Mumbai").
Run the job alert scheduler (e.g., trigger the check manually or let the Cron job run).
The server fetches jobs matching the criteria, caches them, and sends an email.
Run the scheduler a second time.
Observe the server logs: console.log("📧 Sending X jobs to user (deduplication DISABLED)") in backend/src/services/jobFetcher.js.
Check the user's email inbox; a second email is delivered containing the exact same job listings as the first one.

### Expected behavior

he system should query the NotificationLog model to see which of the fetched job listings have already been sent to the user. It should exclude those duplicates and only send an email if there are new job listings. If an email is sent, it should only list the newly discovered jobs.

### Actual behavior

 No deduplication check is made. The processAlert function in 

jobFetcher.js
 directly maps all fetched/cached jobs to the email template. A Mongoose compound unique index on { userId, jobListingId } in NotificationLog throws a duplicate-key error 11000 when trying to log duplicates in the database, but this error is caught and ignored, meaning the email containing the duplicates is still sent.

### Browser / OS

 Node.js 18+ / Backend-only issue (MongoDB + BullMQ + Mongoose)

### Area

Backend

### Expected behavior

ESLint should recognize Vitest globals (describe, test, expect, vi) in test files without any no-undef warnings, since the project already uses Vitest with globals: true in vite.config.js.

### Actual behavior

Running ESLint produces warnings like:

payload.author: vibeetroot
payload.body:
Description
The backend uses BullMQ (backend/src/services/jobAlertQueue.js) with IORedis for background job processing. If the Redis instance is unreachable or REDIS_HOST/REDIS_PORT/REDIS_PASSWORD are missing from the environment, the queue worker fails silently or throws an unhandled error — crashing the entire server startup. This blocks all job alert functionality even when the user only wants non-queue features like resume enhancement or the job tracker.

What to Do

 Wrap Redis/BullMQ initialization in a try/catch with a clear startup warning log
 Allow the server to boot and serve non-queue routes even when Redis is unavailable
 Return a descriptive error ("Job alerts unavailable: Redis not configured") from queue-dependent endpoints instead of crashing
 Add REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, and REDIS_PASSWORD to a .env.example file with comments explaining they are required for job alerts

What NOT to Do

Do NOT silently swallow the Redis connection error,  log a visible warning at startup

Files

backend/src/services/jobAlertQueue.js : add graceful Redis init
backend/src/services/queueManager.js : add availability check before enqueuing
backend/src/index.js : handle queue startup failure without crashing server


Suggested Labels: bug, backend, intermediate
payload.title: [Bug] BullMQ job queue crashes silently when Redis is unavailable

Title: bug: Resolve Cannot access variable before it is declared errors in React components

Description:

markdown
The ESLint output reveals multiple instances of functions or handlers being called inside `useEffect` before their declaration line is parsed. This creates a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) warning/error where variables are accessed out of order.

### Affected Files:
*   `frontend/src/components/CommandPalette.jsx` (Line 153: `handleSelect` is accessed in a `useEffect` handler before it is declared as a `const` at line 164)
*   `frontend/src/components/community/ChatWindow.jsx` (Line 87: `scrollToBottom` accessed before declaration)
*   `frontend/src/components/community/CommentSection.jsx` (Line 181: `fetchComments` accessed before declaration)
*   `frontend/src/components/community/DirectMessages.jsx` (Line 21: `fetchConversations` accessed before declaration)
*   `frontend/src/components/community/PostsFeed.jsx` (Line 69: `fetchPosts` and `fetchScheduledPosts` accessed before declarations)
*   `frontend/src/hooks/useFaceDetection.js` (Line 114: `detectFace` accessed before declaration)

### Expected Behavior / Proposed Fix:
Move the function declarations above the `useEffect` hooks, use standard hoisted function declarations, or wrap handlers inside `useCallback` and position them correctly to make sure the hook dependencies are clean and there are no TDZ execution crashes.

payload.body:
Title: refactor: Fix setState-in-effect violations causing cascading renders in frontend components

### Description:

Currently, the ESLint build fails or emits critical performance warnings across multiple frontend components because `setState` is called synchronously inside `useEffect` hook bodies. According to the official React documentation, calling `setState` synchronously within an effect causes immediate re-renders, hurting application performance and breaking expected lifecycle patterns.

We need to refactor these components to derive their state or safely initialize them.

### Affected Files:
*   `frontend/src/components/CommandPalette.jsx` (Line 101: `setRecentActions(saved)`)
*   `frontend/src/components/FAB.jsx` (Line 58: `setIsOpen(false)`)
*   `frontend/src/components/JobAlertModal.jsx` (Line 27: `setFormData`)
*   `frontend/src/components/ui/AnimatedCounter.jsx` (Line 40: `setDisplay("0")`)
*   `frontend/src/context/AuthContext.jsx` (Line 30: `setLoading(false)`)
*   `frontend/src/hooks/useFaceDetection.js` (Line 162: `initializeDetector()`)

### Expected Behavior:
State values that depend on props or storage should be initialized lazily during state creation (e.g., `useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('recentCommands')) || [])`) rather than using an effect wrapper to synchronize them, or handled inside event handlers.

---

payload.author: thakurakanksha288
payload.body:
### Problem or motivation

Currently, every time a user requests mock interview questions, portfolio feedback, or job tracking updates, the platform hits the backend database or external AI/Job APIs directly. This introduces two major scaling bottlenecks:

High Latency: Waiting on large language model (LLM) processing or external third-party API lookups for common, generic queries (e.g., "Standard behavioral interview questions for Frontend Dev") results in slow page loads.

High API Costs: Redundant requests for identical data consume unnecessary API credits and rate limits.

### Proposed solution

ntroduce a lightweight caching layer (using an in-memory TTL cache like node-cache or a decoupled solution like Redis) to temporarily store frequently accessed, non-user-specific data.

AI Content: Cache common mock interview templates and portfolio structures for 24–48 hours.

Job Tracking/Feeds: Cache external job search results for 1–2 hours so multiple users searching for the same keywords don't trigger constant API rate-limiting.

Cache Invalidation: Implement a straightforward Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration strategy so data naturally refreshes without complex manual invalidation logic.

### Alternatives considered

Implement Static Export Engine (HTML/Markdown) for Generated Portfolios

### Additional context

Do: Wrap the cache logic in a clean, reusable Express middleware so it can easily be toggled on or off for specific API endpoints.

Do: Ensure user-specific private data (like personal resumes or user-specific chat history) is never cached in the shared public pool.

Do Not: Introduce complex cache-busting mechanics; a simple time-based expiration (TTL) is sufficient for this stage of the platform.

### Area

Frontend

payload.author: basantnema31
payload.body:
### Problem Description
As the application grows, the initial bundle size and asset payload increase significantly, leading to slower page load times and degraded performance, especially on mobile devices or slower networks. Currently, it appears that several heavy components, routes, and large image assets are being loaded eagerly during the initial application render.

### The Impact
Eagerly loading all assets and components results in:
1. **Increased Time to Interactive (TTI):** Users have to wait longer before they can interact with the page.
2. **Higher Bandwidth Usage:** Unnecessary resources are downloaded even if the user never navigates to those specific sections of the app.
3. **Lower Lighthouse Scores:** This can negatively impact SEO rankings and overall user experience.

### Proposed Solution
I propose implementing a comprehensive lazy loading strategy across the application:
1. **Component-level Lazy Loading:** Utilize `React.lazy()` and `Suspense` (or dynamic imports in Next.js/Vue depending on the framework) to split the bundle and load heavy components only when they are needed or scrolled into view.
2. **Route-level Code Splitting:** Ensure that routing implements lazy loading so that users only download the JavaScript necessary for the current page.
3. **Image Optimization:** Implement lazy loading for images (e.g., using `loading="lazy"` attribute or an Intersection Observer for custom image components) and ensure images are served in modern formats (like WebP).

### Additional Context
This optimization is crucial for scaling the application and providing a seamless experience for users with varying network speeds.

**Would you please assign this issue to me under the GSSoC '26 program? I would love to work on this and submit a PR.**

*Please add relevant labels such as `gssoc`, `gssoc24`, `hacktoberfest`, `good first issue`, `enhancement`, `performance`, or `level2` if you find this appropriate.*

### What happened?

There are two issues in the current `package.json` file that block the local environment setup and add unnecessary package bloat:

1. **lucide-react Version Blocker:** 
   The dependency `"lucide-react": "^1.17.0"` points to a version that is not yet published to the npm registry (the latest available stable release is `1.16.0`). Because of this, package managers cannot locate the dependency, causing the entire installation process to crash.

2. **Redundant 'cabe' Typo Dependency:**
   Both `"cabe": "^1.0.1"` and `"cobe": "^0.6.5"` are listed under dependencies. `"cobe"` is the correct 3D globe library. The entry for `"cabe"` is a typo that adds unnecessary package bloat and should be removed.

**Proposed Solution:**
- Update `"lucide-react"` to `"^1.16.0"`.
- Delete the `"cabe": "^1.0.1"` line entirely.

### Steps to reproduce

Follow these steps to reproduce the installation failure:

1. Create a clean project folder or clear the `node_modules` directory and delete the `package-lock.json` file if they exist.
2. Ensure the `package.json` contains the following lines:
   ```json
   "cabe": "^1.0.1",
   "lucide-react": "^1.17.0"

### Expected behavior

- Running `npm install` should execute successfully without any errors, installing all dependencies and devDependencies defined in the `package.json` file.
- All listed dependencies should point to valid, published versions on the npm registry.
- Only necessary dependencies are present (specifically, only the correct `"cobe"` library for the 3D globe, without the typo `"cabe"` package).

### Actual behavior

- Running `npm install` fails immediately with an `ETARGET` error because `lucide-react@^1.17.0` does not exist in the npm registry.
- The installation process aborts, leaving the developer unable to install packages, build the application, or start the development server.
- The typo package `"cabe"` is redundantly requested for installation alongside `"cobe"`, which would add unnecessary bloat to the `node_modules` directory if the installation succeeded.

payload.author: printf-sourav
payload.body:
### What happened?

The app has a solid `loginProtection` middleware that locks out IPs after 5 failed attempts on `/login` and `/verify`. However, it is **never applied to `/forgot-password`**. The only protection is a global API limiter of **1000 requests per 15 minutes** — which is so high it provides zero practical protection.

This creates two exploitable problems simultaneously:

**1. Email Spam Attack** — An attacker can flood any user's inbox with hundreds of password reset emails by calling the endpoint in a loop, with no lockout.

**2. Memory Exhaustion (DoS)** — Every call that matches a real email creates a new entry in the in-memory `passwordResetStore` (a `Map`). There is no cap on how many tokens can be generated per email. Hammering the endpoint with a known email will fill server memory and crash the process.

### Steps to reproduce

### Email Spam Attack:

1. Start the server and register an account with any email (e.g. `victim@example.com`).

2. Run this loop from a terminal — no auth required:
for i in {1..50}; do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/forgot-password \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"email": "victim@example.com"}'
done

3. Observe that the victim's inbox receives 50 password reset emails with no lockout or error.

### Memory Exhaustion Attack:

1. Keep the above loop running continuously with thousands of requests.
2. Each iteration adds a new entry to the in-memory passwordResetStore Map.
3. With no cap per email, memory grows unboundedly until the Node.js process crashes with OOM.

### Expected behavior

The `/forgot-password` endpoint should be protected by `loginProtection` middleware (same as `/login`), limiting requests to 5 attempts per IP before a 15-minute lockout. Additionally, only one active reset token should exist per email at a time to prevent memory exhaustion.

### Actual behavior

The `/forgot-password` endpoint should be protected by `loginProtection` middleware (same as `/login`), limiting requests to 5 attempts per IP before a 15-minute lockout. Additionally, only one active reset token should exist per email at a time to prevent memory exhaustion.

### Browser / OS

Node 20 + Ubuntu 22.04 (backend-only issue)

### Area

Backend

### Code of conduct

payload.author: eshaanag
payload.body:
I noticed this while reviewing the portfolio route authorization checks for GSSoC 2026.

Most of the portfolio routes that take `:id` explicitly verify that the authenticated user owns that portfolio id. For example, `POST /api/portfolio/:id/save` checks `req.user.uid !== id` before writing, and the version/restore routes do the same.

The performance endpoint does not have the same ownership guard.

File: `backend/src/routes/portfolio.js`
Line: `496`

```js
router.post(
  '/:id/performance',
  verifyToken,
  asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
    const { id } = req.params;
```

The route is authenticated, but any logged-in user can still submit a request using another user's portfolio id in the URL. Since the handler accepts the `id` directly from `req.params` and returns success for that id, this creates an inconsistent authorization boundary compared to the surrounding portfolio routes.

A realistic way to verify it:
- Log in as user A.
- Send `POST /api/portfolio/<userB-uid>/performance` with a valid metrics payload.
- The route reaches the success response instead of rejecting the request as unauthorized.

Current behavior: the endpoint accepts authenticated requests for arbitrary `:id` values.

Expected behavior: the endpoint should reject requests where `req.user.uid !== id`, the same way `/:id/save`, `/:id/versions`, and `/:id/restore/:versionId` already do.

Why it matters:
- It weakens the portfolio route ownership model.
- It can let one authenticated user write or spoof performance metrics for another user's portfolio.
- It is easy for future code to turn this placeholder response into a real persistence path while keeping the missing guard.

Suggested fix: add an ownership check immediately after reading `id`:

```js
if (req.user.uid !== id) {
  throw new ApiError(403, 'Unauthorized access to this portfolio.');
}
```

It would also be worth adding a regression test that verifies a user cannot submit performance metrics for a different portfolio id.
payload.title: [Security]: Portfolio performance endpoint is missing an ownership check

payload.author: ionfwsrijan
payload.body:
## Problem
When MongoDB is disconnected, portfolio versioning silently falls back to an in-memory `Map`. This introduces:
- silent data loss on restart,
- split-brain behavior across multiple instances,
- inconsistent history/restore semantics depending on connectivity.

This is a critical reliability issue: users can “successfully save” and still lose work.

## Evidence (code)
- In-memory store:
  - `\backend\src\routes\portfolio.js:47`
- Connectivity check and fallback:
  - `\backend\src\routes\portfolio.js:326`
  - `\backend\src\routes\portfolio.js:332`
  - `\backend\src\routes\portfolio.js:404`

## Suggested fix (multi-file, non-trivial)
- Fail closed for versioning when DB is unavailable (503 + clear error), OR
- Provide a durable fallback (Redis / disk-backed) with instance-safe semantics.
- Add telemetry and alerts for DB disconnect.
- Add integration tests:
  - simulate DB down → API rejects saves (or uses durable fallback)
  - multi-instance scenario doesn’t lose versions

## Acceptance criteria
- “Save succeeded” always means durable persistence.
- No environment silently uses in-memory persistence in production mode.
payload.title: Portfolio versioning fails open to in-memory storage (split-brain + silent data loss)

payload.author: ionfwsrijan
payload.body:
## Problem
API keys are “encrypted” on the client using AES with a secret derived from `auth.currentUser.uid`, with a constant fallback secret.

UID is not a secret (it’s visible to the client and often stored/shared), so anyone who can obtain the ciphertext can decrypt it. The constant fallback makes it even weaker.

This provides a false sense of security while still exposing user-provided AI keys to theft.

## Evidence (code)
- Secret derived from uid or constant fallback:
  - `\frontend\src\utils\encryption.js:7`
- Encrypt/decrypt functions:
  - `\frontend\src\utils\encryption.js:14`
  - `\frontend\src\utils\encryption.js:26`

## Suggested fix (multi-file, non-trivial)
- Do not store provider API keys client-side.
- Move BYOK storage server-side:
  - encrypt at rest using server-managed keys (KMS) per user
  - never return raw keys back to frontend
- Replace “send key on each request header” with:
  - server-side key lookup by user identity
- Add migration for existing stored keys and revoke guidance.

## Acceptance criteria
- No user API keys are decryptable using public identifiers (uid) or constants.
- Frontend does not persist provider keys in localStorage/sessionStorage.
- Backend can perform provider calls without requiring plaintext keys from the client on every request.
payload.title: Client-side “encryption” of API keys is reversible (uid/constant secret)

* Screenshot generation should efficiently reuse browser resources

payload.author: techiedevang
payload.body:
What happened?
Summary
While REST API endpoints are protected by Firebase Auth using HTTP headers, the Socket.IO connection initialization does not natively inherit these headers during the WebSocket upgrade request. If the server lacks an explicit io.use() middleware to intercept and validate the Firebase JWT token from the socket's handshake payload, unauthenticated users can establish a direct WebSocket connection. This creates a realtime authentication bypass, allowing unverified clients to connect to the realtime server.

Affected Files

backend/src/config/socket.js (or equivalent backend Socket.IO entry point)

frontend/src/services/socket.js (Client-side connection missing auth payloads)

Root Cause
WebSockets do not automatically send Authorization: Bearer <token> HTTP headers during the protocol upgrade phase the way standard fetch or axios requests do. The Socket.IO server trusts the incoming connection without enforcing a strict token validation handshake. The distinction here is that while the REST architecture (Express) is secured via middleware, the Realtime architecture (Socket.IO) is exposed because it lacks a parallel, connection-level authentication gatekeeper.

Why This Is Difficult To Detect
Most frontend testing happens within an authenticated session, where the client looks completely normal. Furthermore, standard HTTP security audits and automated REST API scanners do not test the WebSocket ws:// or wss:// upgrade lifecycle. Since the main app functions correctly for legitimate users, the open socket goes unnoticed during normal route-level validation.

Production Impact
Unauthenticated scripts or users may be able to:

Connect directly to the realtime server without a valid Firebase account.

Listen to globally broadcasted events (like job alerts or public community updates).

Attempt to emit messages or spoof presence by passing unverified payloads to socket handlers.

Cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by opening thousands of unauthenticated WebSocket connections, exhausting Node.js server memory and Redis subscription limits.

Reproduction

Unauthenticated Connection Setup

Open an external script or API testing tool (like Postman's WebSocket tester).

Do NOT provide any Firebase ID token.

Connect to the WebSocket endpoint (e.g., ws://localhost:5001).

Observe: The connection successfully upgrades and remains open.

Event Listening / Emission

With the unauthenticated socket open, set up a listener for public events.

Observe: Real-time data streams to the unauthenticated client.

Emit a standard client event to a public channel.

Observe: The server processes the unauthenticated connection without immediately dropping it.

Implement io.use((socket, next) => { ... }) middleware on the backend.

Validate the incoming token using firebase-admin.

Reject unauthorized socket operations by calling next(new Error("Authentication error")) and explicitly disconnecting unverified sockets.

Socket connections lacking a valid Firebase token are immediately rejected during the initial handshake.

Socket connections with expired/invalid tokens are rejected.

Valid authenticated users can connect and use realtime features normally.

Regression coverage added for realtime authentication lifecycle behavior.

### What happened?

The Accessibility Checker service currently pollutes Node.js global scope during every accessibility analysis request by attaching JSDOM window objects directly to the global namespace. Additionally, the created JSDOM instances are not properly cleaned up after execution, which can lead to memory leaks and unstable behavior during concurrent requests.

This issue becomes more critical under high traffic or parallel accessibility scans, where multiple requests may overwrite shared global variables and interfere with one another.

Root Cause

In backend/src/services/accessibilityChecker.js, the analyzeAccessibility function dynamically binds JSDOM window variables directly to the Node.js global object:

global.window = window;
global.document = window.document;
global.Node = window.Node;
global.Element = window.Element;
global.HTMLElement = window.HTMLElement;

This creates:

global namespace pollution
possible race conditions during parallel execution
memory leaks due to missing JSDOM cleanup

Suggested Fix
Avoid mutating the Node.js global object directly
Use isolated axe-core execution contexts where possible
Properly cleanup JSDOM instances using:
window.close()
Restore/remove temporary global bindings after execution
Ensure thread-safe concurrent execution behavior

### Steps to reproduce

1.Trigger the accessibility analysis endpoint multiple times concurrently
2.Observe memory usage and execution behavior
3.Monitor Node.js process memory and global object mutations
4.Run repeated scans over time

### Expected behavior

Accessibility analysis should run in an isolated execution context
JSDOM instances should be properly cleaned up after analysis
Global Node.js scope should remain untouched
Concurrent requests should execute safely without race conditions or shared-state interference

### Actual behavior

Global variables such as window, document, Node, and HTMLElement are overwritten during each request
JSDOM instances remain uncleared after execution
Concurrent executions may interfere with each other
Memory usage may continuously increase over time due to improper cleanup

### Browser / OS

OS : Backend / node.js environment

payload.author: eshaanag
payload.body:
While tracing the Socket.IO channel flow for GSSoC 2026, I noticed that the same `join_channel` event is registered in two places for the same socket connection.

The first registration happens inside the shared socket handlers:

File: `backend/src/services/socketServiceFirebase.js`
Line: `31`

```js
socket.on('join_channel', async (channelId) => {
```

Then `backend/src/config/socket.js` calls `setupSocketHandlers(io, socket)` and immediately registers another handler for the same event:

File: `backend/src/config/socket.js`
Lines: `48` and `51`

```js
setupSocketHandlers(io, socket);

socket.on('join_channel', async (channelId) => {
```

That means a single client emit can run two different code paths:
- one path loads the channel document and emits `user_joined_channel`
- the second path joins presence and emits another `user_joined_channel`

In practice, this can cause duplicate join notifications, duplicate room/presence work, and harder-to-debug realtime behavior because the same event name has two owners.

How I would verify it:
- Connect a socket with auth.
- Emit `join_channel` once from the client.
- Watch backend logs or client listeners for `user_joined_channel`.
- The event can be processed by both handlers instead of one clear channel join path.

Expected result: `join_channel` should have one source of truth that handles room join, presence, validation, and notification consistently.

Current result: the event is split across two handlers, so the same user action can perform duplicate work.

Suggested fix: keep a single `join_channel` handler. Either move the presence call into `setupSocketHandlers`, or remove the inline handler from `backend/src/config/socket.js` and let the service-level handler own the flow. The final handler should also keep the channel existence check before joining presence.
payload.title: [Bug]: join_channel socket event is registered twice

payload.author: eshaanag
payload.body:
I hit this while checking the community channel creation path for GSSoC 2026.

`createChannel` reads `name` from `req.body`, but it normalizes the value before doing any validation:

```js
const channelName = name.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, '-');
```

File: `backend/src/controllers/communityFirebaseController.js`
Line: `98`

If the request body is missing `name`, or if `name` is not a string, the handler throws a raw `TypeError` before it can return a clean validation response. That means a malformed client request can skip the intended API error flow and turn into a 500-style failure.

Why this matters:
- A simple bad request can crash this controller path before validation.
- API consumers get an internal error instead of a clear `400 Bad Request`.
- It also makes later duplicate-name checks unreliable because the input is never safely normalized.

One quick way to verify:
1. Send a create-channel request without `name`, or with `name: null`.
2. The handler reaches line 98 and attempts `name.toLowerCase()`.
3. The request fails before a useful validation error can be returned.

Current behavior: invalid `name` values throw before validation.

Expected behavior: the route should validate `name` first, return a clear 400 response for missing/invalid names, and only normalize after confirming it is a non-empty string.

A practical fix would be to add an early guard before line 98, for example checking `typeof name === 'string' && name.trim()`, then normalize with `name.trim().toLowerCase().replace(...)`.
payload.title: [Bug]: Community channel creation crashes when name is missing

payload.body:
### What happened?

In LinkedInCallback.jsx, the token exchange callback hook does not safeguard against multiple mounts. Under React 18/19 development environments where <React.StrictMode> is enabled, components mount, unmount, and remount instantly. Because the component triggers the token exchange fetch call to the backend on mount without verifying if a request is already active or completed, it fires two requests with the same authorization code.

The first request succeeds and burns the one-time authorization code, but the second request fails because the code has already been used. This triggers the catch block in the second request, causing the sign-in flow to abort, show an error toast, and redirect the user back to the login page.

(Note: Other callback pages in the project, such as OpenRouterCallback.jsx, correctly use an isProcessing ref safeguard to prevent this double-mount behavior).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Go to the login page at /login in a local development environment (where React StrictMode is active).
2. Click on the Sign in with LinkedIn button.
3. Authenticate and authorize the application on the LinkedIn consent screen.
4. LinkedIn redirects you back to /auth/linkedin/callback?code=YOUR_AUTH_CODE .
5. See the callback loading state briefly, then see a "Failed to sign in. Please try again." toast error, and get redirected back to /login .

### Expected behavior

The token exchange flow should be guarded (e.g., using a useRef flag or an AbortController) so that only one request is sent to the backend. The user should be logged in successfully and redirected to /dashboard (or prompted for 2FA if enabled).

### Actual behavior

The duplicate fetch call in StrictMode uses the same LinkedIn one-time code twice, causing the second call to fail, which triggers a redirect back to /login and shows a toast error.

### Browser / OS

OS: Windows 11, Browser: Chrome, Version: 122

### Area

Frontend

## 🐛 Security Bug

### Description
The password reset flow generates a token sent via email. However, once used (or if unused), 
the token is **not invalidated or expired server-side**. This means:

1. A used password reset link can be replayed to reset the password again
2. Old reset emails in a user's inbox remain permanently exploitable
3. No time-based expiry enforced beyond what's in the JWT payload (if any)

### Proposed Fix
- Store reset tokens in MongoDB `User` model with fields:
```javascript
  passwordResetToken: String,       // hashed token
  passwordResetExpires: Date,       // Date.now() + 10 minutes
  passwordResetUsed: Boolean        // mark as used after consumption
```
- On token verification: check `resetExpires > Date.now()` AND `resetUsed === false`
- On successful reset: set `passwordResetUsed = true` and clear `passwordResetToken`

### Impact
🔴 **Critical** — Account takeover risk via replayed or leaked reset links.

### Labels
`bug` `security` `backend` `critical`

## 🐛 Security Bug

### Description
The resume upload endpoint (`/api/resume/upload`) relies only on **client-side validation** for 
file type and size. The backend middleware in `backend/src/middleware/` does not validate:

- ✅ File MIME type (only PDF/DOCX should be allowed)
- ✅ File size limit enforcement at the server level
- ✅ File content inspection (magic bytes check)

An attacker can bypass the frontend and directly POST any file (`.exe`, `.sh`, malicious HTML) 
to the endpoint using tools like `curl` or Postman.

### Steps to Reproduce
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.careerpilot.com/api/resume/upload \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <valid_token>" \
  -F "file=@malicious.exe"
```
Upload succeeds without rejection.

### Proposed Fix
- In `backend/src/middleware/upload.js` (multer config), add:
  - `fileFilter` to check `mimetype` against allowlist: `['application/pdf', 'application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document']`
  - `limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }` (5MB max)
- Add a magic-bytes check using the `file-type` npm package for server-side MIME verification

### Impact
🔴 **Critical** — Arbitrary file upload is a top-10 OWASP vulnerability.

### Labels
`bug` `security` `backend` `critical`

## 🐛 Bug Report

### Description
The AI-powered endpoints (resume enhancement, mock interview, portfolio AI enhance) that call 
the Google Gemini 2.5 API have **no per-user rate limiting**. This creates two critical problems:

1. **Cost explosion**: A single user or bot can spam the `/api/resume/enhance` or `/api/ai/*` 
   endpoints thousands of times, generating massive Gemini API bills.
2. **DoS vector**: Flooding the AI endpoints can exhaust the API quota, making the service

### Current State

- Add a **per-user, per-endpoint rate limiter** using `express-rate-limit` + Redis store
- Suggested limits: max 5 AI requests/minute per user, 50/day
- Return `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header
- Track usage in Redis with user ID as key

## 🐛 Bug Report / Security Issue

### Description
Currently, when a user logs out, the JWT token is only removed from the client side (localStorage/cookie). 
However, the token remains valid on the server until it naturally expires. This means:
- A stolen token can still be used to authenticate after logout
- No way to force-logout a user session remotely
- Violates OWASP session management guidelines

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Login and copy the Bearer token from DevTools > Network
2. Logout from the UI
3. Use the copied token in Postman to hit any protected API endpoint
4. ✅ Request succeeds — token is still valid

### Expected Behavior
After logout, the token should be **blacklisted server-side** (e.g., stored in Redis with TTL matching token expiry) 
and any request with a blacklisted token should return `401 Unauthorized`.

### Proposed Fix
- Create a Redis-based token blacklist in `backend/src/config/`
- On logout, add the token's `jti` (or full token hash) to Redis with TTL = token expiry
- Add middleware to check blacklist before processing protected routes

### Impact
🔴 **Critical** — Session hijacking risk. Any user whose token is intercepted remains vulnerable post-logout.

### Labels
`bug` `security` `backend` `critical`


I would like to work on this under GSSoC
/assign
payload.title: [Security] JWT tokens remain valid after logout — no server-side invalidation

Problem or motivation
Currently, users can trigger multiple AI generation requests (resume suggestions, interview feedback, or content generation) by clicking the generate button repeatedly in quick succession.

Duplicate API calls
Increased server load
Multiple inconsistent responses rendering together
Poor user experience due to accidental repeated submissions

Implement a debounce/locking mechanism for AI action buttons.

Suggested behavior:

Disable the generate button immediately after click
Re-enable it once the request completes or fails
Optionally show a loading indicator/spinner while processing
Prevent duplicate API calls from rapid repeated clicks
This should be applied consistently across AI-powered sections such as:

Resume optimization
Mock interview generation
Portfolio/content generation
AI suggestions
Alternatives considered
Users can currently avoid repeated clicks manually, but this is unreliable and does not prevent accidental duplicate requests.

Additional context
This is a beginner-friendly frontend enhancement that improves UX, reduces unnecessary backend load, and prevents duplicate AI responses. Similar debounce behavior is commonly implemented in AI-based platforms and form submission workflows.

### Problem or motivation

The current `test.js` integration runner has a few issues that affect developer experience and CI reliability:

- `process.exit(0)` always exits with success even when tests fail — CI pipelines cannot detect broken services
- MongoDB connection has no timeout, so a wrong URI causes the process to hang indefinitely
- No response time tracking — no way to know if a service is slow vs completely down
- Repetitive try/catch blocks make the file harder to maintain

### Proposed solution

Refactor `test.js` with the following improvements:

- Add a reusable `runTest(name, fn)` wrapper that handles timing and error catching for every service
- Track response time per service using `performance.now()`
- Print a summary table at the end showing pass/fail status, response time, and detail for each service
- Fix exit code: `process.exit(1)` when any service fails, `process.exit(0)` only when all pass
- Add `serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000` to MongoDB connect so it fails fast
- Add `timeout: 8000` to the RapidAPI Axios call for the same reason

### Alternatives considered

Could use a test framework like Jest or Vitest, but that adds unnecessary dependencies for a simple connectivity check script. The proposed change keeps it lightweight with no new dependencies.

### Additional context

This is a pure refactor — no changes to any service logic, APIs, or environment variables. 
Only `test.js` is modified. Safe to merge without risk of breaking existing functionality.

### Area

Backend

## Feature Description

A new **Repo Health Scorer** under the GitHub Intelligence module that analyzes any public GitHub repository and produces a comprehensive health score (0–100) with a detailed breakdown across multiple quality dimensions. Users paste a GitHub repo URL, and the system returns an overall score, per-dimension sub-scores, signal data, and actionable suggestions for improvement.

This aligns with the existing `backend/src/services/github/repoHealthScorer.js` and `frontend/src/components/github/HealthScoreGauge.jsx` slots already referenced in `CONTRIBUTION.md`.

## Problem It Solves

Developers, recruiters, and students evaluating open-source projects (for contribution, dependency choice, or learning) currently have no quick, objective way to assess repo quality. They have to manually check the README, last commit date, issue activity, contributor count, license presence, etc. This feature automates that evaluation and surfaces concrete improvement suggestions directly aligned with CareerPilot's mission of helping users build strong portfolios and contribute meaningfully to open source.

For CareerPilot users specifically, this becomes a tool to:
- Audit their own repositories before listing them on a portfolio
- Evaluate repos before contributing during GSSoC / Hacktoberfest / open source events
- Identify weak spots in their public GitHub presence

## Proposed Solution

### Scoring Dimensions (weighted)

| Dimension | Weight | Signals |
|---|---|---|
| **Activity** | 25% | Commits in last 30/90 days, last commit recency, open vs closed PR ratio |
| **Community** | 20% | Stars, forks, contributors count, issue response time |
| **Documentation** | 20% | README quality & length, presence of LICENSE / CONTRIBUTING / CODE_OF_CONDUCT, repo description, topics |
| **Code Quality** | 20% | Test files/folders present, CI config (`.github/workflows`), releases/tags, language diversity |
| **Maintenance** | 15% | Open issues age, stale PRs, dependabot/security config |

Each dimension returns `{ score: 0-100, signals: [...], suggestions: [...] }`. Overall score is a weighted average.

### API Endpoint
GET /api/github/health-score?url=<github-repo-url>
Response:
```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "repo": { "owner": "...", "name": "...", "url": "..." },
    "overallScore": 78,
    "grade": "B+",
    "dimensions": {
      "activity": { "score": 85, "signals": {...}, "suggestions": [...] },
      "community": { "score": 70, ... },
      "documentation": { "score": 90, ... },
      "codeQuality": { "score": 65, ... },
      "maintenance": { "score": 75, ... }
    },
    "topSuggestions": ["Add a LICENSE file", "Your last release was 8 months ago", ...],
    "analyzedAt": "2026-05-27T..."
  }
}
```

Auth-protected via existing `verifyToken` middleware. Cached for 1 hour to respect GitHub's rate limits (60/hr unauthenticated, 5000/hr with token).

- **Components:**
  - `HealthScoreGauge.jsx` — animated circular gauge for the overall score

  - `SuggestionsList.jsx` — actionable improvement suggestions card
- Mobile-responsive, follows existing dark theme + design tokens
- New nav entry under the GitHub section

- **A single composite "stars + forks" score** — rejected as too shallow; the value here is the dimension breakdown and actionable suggestions.
- **Real-time scoring on every page load** — rejected in favor of 1-hour caching for rate-limit safety and performance.

### What happened?

## Summary

Several Socket.IO realtime handlers authenticate users successfully but do not verify ownership or membership for the conversation/channel/room identifiers they operate on.

As a result, authenticated users can interact with arbitrary conversations, fellowship rooms, and private channels simply by supplying known identifiers.

This creates a realtime authorization bypass affecting messaging and protected collaboration flows.

---

## Affected Files

- `socketServiceFirebase.js`
- `communityFirebaseController.js`

---

## Root Cause

Socket authentication currently validates that the user is logged in, but multiple handlers trust client-supplied identifiers without enforcing membership validation.

Examples include:

- direct message conversation access
- fellowship room joins
- private channel messaging
- private channel message retrieval

Patterns similar to:

```js
socket.emit("send_direct_message", {
  conversationId,
  ...
})
```

proceed without verifying:

```js
conversation.participantIds.includes(user.uid)
```

Similarly, fellowship and channel socket flows trust arbitrary room/channel ids once authentication succeeds.

This creates a distinction between:

- authentication
- and authorization

where users are authenticated but not properly authorized for the target resource.

---

## Why This Is Difficult To Detect

REST endpoints often perform ownership checks correctly, which creates the appearance that access control is implemented consistently.

However, the realtime Socket.IO paths bypass many of the invariants enforced in REST flows.

Because most tests focus on route-level behavior rather than websocket lifecycle behavior, the issue remains hidden during normal validation.

---

## Production Impact

Authenticated users may be able to:

- inject messages into other users’ conversations
- read private fellowship chats
- access private community channels
- corrupt unread counts
- pollute conversation state
- observe unauthorized realtime activity

This affects core messaging and collaboration security guarantees.

---

### Direct Message Injection

1. Authenticate with any valid Firebase token
2. Obtain or guess another conversation id
3. Emit:

```js

```

with the foreign `conversationId`

Observe:

- unauthorized conversation interaction succeeds

- unauthorized room join succeeds

Observe unauthorized access succeeds without verified membership enforcement.

---

All realtime handlers should enforce membership validation before:

- joining rooms
- reading messages

Recommended approach:

- centralize membership/ownership checks
- validate conversation/channel/room membership server-side
- reject unauthorized socket operations consistently with REST access rules

---

- users can only interact with conversations they belong to
- fellowship room membership is enforced
- private channel membership is enforced
- unauthorized socket events are rejected
- regression coverage added for realtime authorization behavior

---

Critical

2. Obtain or guess another valid:

### What happened?

## Summary

The proposal escrow/payment flow validates only the Razorpay HMAC signature but does not verify that the payment actually belongs to the server-created proposal/order/challenge state.

Additionally, proposal acceptance can still occur through the fellowship proposal status endpoint without any verified escrow payment.

This allows proposal/payment state corruption and escrow bypass despite apparently valid payment verification logic.

---

## Affected Files

- `payments.js`
- `paymentService.js`
- `fellowships.js`

---

## Root Cause

The current payment verification flow validates only:

```txt
order_id | payment_id
```

using the Razorpay HMAC signature.

However, the implementation does not:

- fetch and validate the Razorpay order/payment server-side
- bind payments to the original proposal
- verify expected amount
- verify challenge ownership/state
- validate Razorpay payment status
- validate notes/metadata linkage

Separately:

```http
PUT /api/fellowship/proposals/:id/status
```

can still mark proposals as accepted and create fellowship chat rooms without any verified escrow completion.

This creates a cross-route invariant failure where:

- payment verification
- proposal acceptance
- escrow state
- and fellowship activation

can become desynchronized.

---

## Why This Is Difficult To Detect

At first glance, the flow appears secure because:

- Razorpay signature verification exists
- ownership checks exist
- proposal state checks exist

However, the missing invariant is cross-request validation.

The backend never proves that:

- the verified payment belongs to the proposal being accepted
- the payment amount matches
- the payment corresponds to the intended challenge
- or the proposal acceptance path actually requires escrow completion

Each isolated flow appears correct individually, but together they allow forged escrow state transitions.

---

## Production Impact

A malicious or compromised user could:

- mark proposals as escrowed using unrelated valid payments
- bypass escrow entirely
- create fellowship chat rooms without payment
- corrupt proposal/payment state
- gain unauthorized access to challenge workflows
- trigger inconsistent business/payment records

This affects core payment and collaboration flows.

---

## Reproduction

### Escrow Forgery Path

1. Create a pending proposal for a high-value challenge
2. Obtain any valid Razorpay success tuple under the same merchant account
3. Submit the tuple to the payment verification flow
4. Observe proposal/payment state transition succeeds despite unrelated payment context

### Direct Acceptance Bypass

Issue:

```http
PUT /api/fellowship/proposals/:id/status
```

with:

```json
{
  "status": "accepted"
}
```

Observe:
- proposal accepted
- fellowship/chat room created
- no verified escrow enforcement

---

## Proposed Fix

The backend should:

- persist server-created payment/order metadata
- fetch and validate Razorpay payment/order state server-side
- bind payments to:
  - proposal id
  - challenge id
  - expected amount
  - expected payer/payee
- require verified escrow completion before proposal acceptance
- reject proposal state transitions lacking validated payment linkage

---

## Acceptance Criteria

- payment verification is bound to the originating proposal/order
- unrelated valid Razorpay payments cannot be reused
- proposal acceptance requires verified escrow completion
- challenge/payment/proposal state remains synchronized
- regression coverage added for cross-route payment invariants

---

## Severity

Critical

This is a business-critical payment integrity flaw affecting escrow enforcement, proposal state correctness, and protected fellowship workflows.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a pending fellowship proposal tied to a challenge requiring escrow/payment verification.

2. Obtain any valid Razorpay success tuple (`razorpay_order_id`, `razorpay_payment_id`, `razorpay_signature`) under the same merchant a

payload.body:
**Describe the Bug**
The current snapshot tests rely on shared mutable state (lastMailOptions) across multiple async test cases. This can cause flaky or incorrect snapshot assertions if tests run concurrently or if one test mutates the shared state before another assertion executes.
Additionally:
- process.env.EMAIL_SERVICE_URL and process.env.EMAIL_API_KEY are globally overwritten without restoring original values after the test suite.
- The mock transport does not validate whether expected email fields (to, subject, html) are actually passed.
- The tests only snapshot html content and do not verify important metadata like recipient or subject line.
- Failures inside one nested test may leave stale lastMailOptions data for subsequent tests.
This reduces test reliability and may hide regressions in email generation logic.

**Steps to Reproduce**
1. Run the snapshot tests together with other async mail-service tests.
2. Introduce parallel execution or another test that also modifies the mock transport.
3. Observe intermittent snapshot mismatches or reused lastMailOptions values.
4. Modify a template subject/recipient while keeping HTML unchanged.
5. Notice that tests still pass despite metadata regressions.

**Expected Behavior**
1. Each test should use isolated mail payload state.
2. Environment variables modified during tests should be restored afterward.
3. Email metadata (to, subject) should also be validated.
4. Mock transport should fail fast when required fields are missing.
5. Snapshot assertions should remain deterministic under parallel execution.

**Additional Context**
These changes improve snapshot determinism, reduce flaky async behavior, and ensure email template regressions are caught more accurately during CI runs.
payload.title: Improve reliability and isolation in email template snapshot tests

payload.author: chirag-gupta-07
payload.body:
### Problem or motivation

Implement an intelligent, action-taking AI chatbot within the Career Pilot project. Rather than just offering advice, this AI will utilize Function/Tool Calling to actively help users build their portfolio by injecting data (like education, skills, and projects) directly into the application state based on the conversation.

### Proposed solution

💡 Proposed Solution & Architecture
To achieve this, we will implement an Agentic AI Architecture using the Vercel AI SDK alongside our React frontend. The solution is broken down into three main layers:

1. The Interface Layer (React/Frontend)
We will introduce a new ChatAssistant component. This component will use the Vercel AI SDK's useChat hook, which automatically handles message state, loading states, and text streaming. Crucially, the frontend will be responsible for executing the actions. When the AI decides to call a tool, the frontend will map that tool call to our existing React state-management functions (e.g., triggering the same dispatch or setState that our standard forms use).

2. The API / Proxy Layer (Backend/Server)
To maintain security, the frontend will never communicate directly with the AI provider. We will create a secure backend endpoint (e.g., /api/chat).

This endpoint will hold the secure API keys (like GEMINI_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY).
It will receive the user's conversation history, append our System Prompt (which tells the AI its identity and rules), and forward the request to the AI model.
It will utilize streamText to send the response back to the client in real-time chunks.
3. The Tooling Layer (Function Calling mechanism)
This is the core of the proposed solution. When we initialize the AI on the backend, we will pass it a strictly typed schema (using Zod) of the actions it is allowed to take.

Example Workflow:

User types: "I went to MIT from 2020 to 2024."
AI Processing: The AI evaluates the prompt and recognizes it has a tool called add_education that matches this intent.
Tool Execution: Instead of just replying with text, the AI generates a JSON payload: { "tool": "add_education", "args": { "school": "MIT", "startDate": "2020", "endDate": "2024" } }
State Update: The frontend intercepts this tool call, automatically updates the user's portfolio preview on the screen, and the AI follows up with a confirmation message: "I've added MIT to your education section!"
By decoupling the AI reasoning from the UI state updates, we ensure the application remains fast, deterministic, and highly interactive.

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

_No response_

Other

payload.author: dhanasai2
payload.body:
##  Feature Description

Currently, after completing a mock interview session, users receive individual question scores and feedback. However, there is **no aggregated AI-generated skill gap summary** that tells the user:

- Which skills/topics they performed weakest in
- What they should study or practice next
- An overall readiness score breakdown by category (e.g., technical, behavioral, communication)

This makes it hard for users to take action after their interview session ends.

---

##  Proposed Solution

After the interview is completed (when `POST /api/interview/:id/complete` is called), the backend should:

1. Collect all per-question AI evaluation results already stored in the session
2. Pass them to the Gemini AI with a prompt asking for a concise **skill gap analysis**
3. Return a structured `skillGapSummary` field in the completion response

On the **frontend** (`InterviewPrep.jsx` or a new `InterviewResult.jsx`), display:
- A **"Skill Gap Summary" card** with:
  - Top 3 weak areas (e.g., "System Design", "Problem Solving under pressure")
  - 2–3 recommended next steps (e.g., "Practice LeetCode Medium DP problems")
  - An overall readiness label: `Beginner / Developing / Interview-Ready`

---

##  Files to Modify

- `backend/src/services/interviewService.js` — add skill gap prompt to Gemini after session ends
- `backend/src/routes/interview.js` — include `skillGapSummary` in the complete endpoint response
- `frontend/src/pages/InterviewPrep.jsx` — render the new summary card in the results view

---

##  Why This is Beginner-Friendly

- The Gemini API call pattern already exists in the codebase (resume enhancement uses the same approach)
- No new packages or infrastructure needed
- Logic is self-contained: read existing scores → prompt Gemini → return structured text
- Frontend card is a simple UI component using existing Tailwind styles

---

##  Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] After interview completion, `skillGapSummary` is present in the API response
- [ ] Gemini prompt asks for weak skill areas and next steps based on all answer evaluations
- [ ] Frontend displays the Skill Gap Summary card after results load
- [ ] The card shows: weak areas, recommended actions, and readiness label
- [ ] No breaking changes to existing interview history or scoring

---

##  Suggested Labels
`enhancement`, `ai/ml`, `beginner`, `good first issue`, `backend`, `frontend` , 'GSSOC:approved'

---

_I would love to work on this issue as part of GSSoC. Can I be assigned? I am comfortable with Node.js, Express, and React, and eager to learn how to work with Gemini API prompting._
payload.title: [Feature] [AI] Add Skill Gap Summary Card at End of Mock Interview Session

payload.author: knoxiboy
payload.body:
## Description

In `frontend/src/components/Navbar.jsx`, both the **search suggestions dropdown** (line 141-166) and the **user profile dropdown** (line 240-293) are controlled by the same `showDropdown` boolean state variable (line 34).

This means:
- Clicking the user profile avatar while the search input is focused **closes** the search dropdown **and simultaneously opens** the user menu (or vice versa).
- The `onFocus` of the search input sets `showDropdown = true`, which also accidentally opens the user profile dropdown if it was closed.
- `onBlur` on the search input closes the user dropdown too.

Both components are fighting over the same shared boolean, leading to unpredictable dropdown behavior.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Log in to Career Pilot.
2. Click on the search input in the navbar.
3. While the search suggestions dropdown is visible, click the user avatar/profile button.
4. Both dropdowns flash and behave erratically.

## Expected Behavior
The search dropdown and user profile dropdown should operate independently.

## Proposed Fix
Separate the state into two independent booleans:

```diff
- const [showDropdown, setShowDropdown] = useState(false)
+ const [showSearchDropdown, setShowSearchDropdown] = useState(false)
+ const [showProfileDropdown, setShowProfileDropdown] = useState(false)
```

Then update the search input's `onFocus`/`onBlur` to use `setShowSearchDropdown`, and the profile button's `onClick` to use `setShowProfileDropdown`.

---
**Note:** I would love to fix this bug! Please assign this issue to me.
payload.title: [Bug]: Navbar search suggestions dropdown conflicts with user profile dropdown — both share the same 'showDropdown' state

## Description

In `frontend/src/components/Navbar.jsx` (line 35), the notification count is initialized as a static constant:

```jsx
const [notificationCount] = useState(3)
```

This value is never updated — it uses `useState` without a setter function, meaning the red badge in the navbar **always shows '3'** regardless of whether the user has any actual notifications. This is misleading UX and may confuse users into thinking they have unread notifications.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Log in to any account on Career Pilot.
2. Observe the notification bell icon in the navbar.
3. The badge always shows '3' even on a fresh account with no activity.

## Expected Behavior
- The notification badge should reflect the actual unread notification count.
- If there are zero notifications, the badge should be hidden entirely.
- At minimum, the hardcoded value should be replaced with `0` until a real notification system is wired up.

## Proposed Fix
Either:
1. **Quick fix**: Change the default to `0` so the badge doesn't show false information: `const [notificationCount] = useState(0)`
2. **Better fix**: Wire the notification count to a real data source (API call or context) and include the setter: `const [notificationCount, setNotificationCount] = useState(0)`

---
**Note:** I would love to fix this bug! Please assign this issue to me.

payload.author: pushpit21jain
payload.body:
## 📝 Issue Description
Currently, when the backend dispatches heavy background tasks (such as AI resume enhancement or ATS score analysis) to the BullMQ job queues, it directly calls the Google Gemini 2.5 API. If the Gemini API experiences high latency, hits rate limits, or times out, the queue worker fails abruptly. 

This can lead to unhandled promise rejections, stalled jobs in Redis, or an inconsistent state where the user's dashboard UI hangs indefinitely waiting for a real-time completion event via Socket.IO.

## 🎯 Proposed Solution / Enhancement
- **Implement Robust Try-Catch Blocks:** Wrap the Gemini API calls inside `backend/src/services/` (or the respective queue worker process) with explicit error handling.
- **Graceful Retries with Exponential Backoff:** Configure BullMQ job options to attempt a fixed number of retries with a backoff strategy when dealing with transient external API errors (e.g., rate limits or network hiccups).
- **Fallback Status Updates:** If a job completely fails after maximum retries, catch the error globally in the worker, update the database status (e.g., `failed`), and emit a failure event via Socket.IO to notify the frontend dynamically.

## 🛠️ Affected Tech Stack / Components
- [ ] **Frontend:** (React 19, TailwindCSS 4, Vite)
- [x] **Backend:** (Node.js, Express, MongoDB)
- [x] **Infrastructure/Queues:** (Redis, BullMQ)
- [x] **AI Integration:** (Google Gemini 2.5)

## 🔄 Steps to Reproduce (If Bug)
1. Trigger an asynchronous AI task (e.g., upload a complex resume and request an ATS analysis).
2. Simulate a network drop or manually inject an invalid/expired `GEMINI_API_KEY` into the backend `.env`.
3. Monitor the backend logs; the BullMQ job worker throws a failure without cleanly closing the job or alerting the user.
4. Observe that the UI spinner continues indefinitely.

## 📸 Screenshots / Logs (Optional)
payload.title: fix(backend): handle Google Gemini API timeouts and queue failures gracefully in BullMQ workers

The AI provider configuration files use environment variables such as process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY directly without validating whether the keys exist. genAI.js
aiProviders.js

This creates instability in:

AI endpoints
resume enhancement features
content generation flows
onboarding/setup for contributors

OS: Fedora Linux
Browser: Firefox / Brave

### Problem or motivation

Currently, most career platforms only help users create resumes, analyze ATS scores, or match jobs. However, users still struggle with the real-world hiring journey after applying.

Candidates often do not know:

whether they are interview-ready,
which hiring stage they may fail at,
how their profile compares against real hiring expectations,
or which exact skills are blocking them from progressing further.

This especially affects students, freshers, and early-career developers who need structured career guidance beyond resume optimization.

An intelligent career simulation system would help users visualize their hiring journey, identify weak areas, and receive actionable improvement recommendations before applying to jobs.

### Proposed solution

Implement an AI-Powered Career Simulation & Interview Progression System that simulates a realistic hiring pipeline based on:

uploaded resume,
selected job role,
ATS score,
technical skills,
projects,
and experience level.

Generate a simulated recruitment pipeline such as:

Resume Screening
Online Assessment
Technical Interview
System Design Round
HR Round
Final Selection

Each stage should display:

estimated success probability,
detected weak points,
required skills,
and personalized improvement suggestions.
2. Skill Gap Heatmap

Visual dashboard showing:

strong skills,
missing technologies,
communication gaps,
project depth analysis,
interview readiness indicators.
3. AI Career Roadmap Generator

Generate a personalized roadmap:

skills to learn,
recommended projects,
certifications,
interview preparation strategy,
estimated readiness timeline.

Predict possible rejection reasons such as:

weak project complexity,
insufficient backend depth,
missing deployment experience,
low DSA readiness,
poor resume keyword coverage,
lack of measurable achievements.

Allow users to:

save simulation history,
compare improvements over time,
track interview readiness score evolution.
Technical Notes

Possible implementation ideas:

Gemini/OpenAI-based analysis
Resume parsing pipeline
Skill extraction with embeddings/NLP
Dynamic scoring engine
Radar charts / heatmaps for visualization
Timeline-based career progression UI
Zustand/Redux state management
Supabase/Firebase/PostgreSQL persistence layer

### Alternatives considered

Simple ATS score systems
Static resume feedback modules
Manual interview preparation checklists

These approaches do not provide a complete end-to-end hiring journey simulation or actionable career progression insights.

### Additional context

This feature would transform Career Pilot from a resume-analysis tool into a complete AI-powered career growth platform.

Potential future expansions:

mock interview integration,
recruiter benchmarking,
peer comparison analytics,
real-world hiring trend analysis,
AI-generated interview question sets.

Payment APIs should remain fully operational.

Payment routes disabled: Identifier 'razorpay' has already been declared

As a consequence:

payment routes fail to initialize
Razorpay integration becomes unavailable
payment-related functionality is effectively broken

---

### 🎯 What You're Building

Build a **complete, single-page portfolio website** with the **Netflix Browse** theme.

> Netflix browse UI with horizontal carousels of project cards, hover expansion with preview details, featured hero banner at top, dark background.

> **You MUST work strictly in this folder — do not create files outside of it.**

```
frontend/src/components/portfolio/templates/Netflix_Browse/index.jsx

Your main component export must be in `index.jsx`. You may create additional sub-components in the same folder (e.g., `Hero.jsx`, `Projects.jsx`) and import them into `index.jsx`.

**Folder structure example:**
```
frontend/src/components/portfolio/templates/Netflix_Browse/
├── index.jsx          ← Main export (REQUIRED)
├── Hero.jsx           ← Optional sub-component
├── Projects.jsx       ← Optional sub-component
└── styles.css         ← Optional (prefer Tailwind)
```

---

### 📊 Data Source

All portfolio data comes from a **single shared JSON file**. Import it like this:

```jsx
import data from '../../../../data/dummy_data.json';
```

**Available data fields:**
- `data.personal` — name, title, bio, avatar, location
- `data.socials` — github, linkedin, twitter, email
- `data.skills` — array of { name, level, category }
- `data.projects` — array of { title, description, techStack, liveUrl, githubUrl, image }
- `data.experience` — array of { role, company, period, description }
- `data.testimonials` — array of { name, role, text, avatar }
- `data.stats` — yearsExperience, projectsCompleted, happyClients

**⚠️ Do NOT hardcode portfolio data.** Always read from the JSON file so templates work with any user's data.

---

### ✅ Technical Requirements

| Requirement | Details |
|---|---|
| **Framework** | React (JSX) |
| **Styling** | Tailwind CSS (utility classes). No external CSS frameworks. |
| **Responsiveness** | Must look great on mobile, tablet, and desktop |
| **Icons** | Use `lucide-react` for icons |
| **Images** | Use the image URLs from `dummy_data.json`. Use CSS/SVG for decorative elements |
| **Animations** | Use `framer-motion` for animations (already installed) |
| **Standalone** | Component must be modular and self-contained in its folder |
| **No Hardcoded Data** | All content must come from `dummy_data.json` |

---

### 🚀 How to Claim This Issue

1. **Comment `.take` on this issue** to claim it
2. **Fork** the repository
3. Run `cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev`
4. Edit the placeholder file at `frontend/src/components/portfolio/templates/Netflix_Browse/index.jsx`
5. Build the complete portfolio template
6. Submit a **Pull Request**

---

### 📸 MANDATORY: Screenshots Required

> **⚠️ Your PR will NOT be merged without screenshots.**

You **MUST** include in your PR description:
- 📱 **Mobile screenshot** (375px width)
- 💻 **Desktop screenshot** (1440px width)
- 🎬 **Screen recording** (optional but highly encouraged for animated templates)

---

### 🏷️ Labels
`good first issue` • `portfolio-template` • `react` • `hacktoberfest`

Let's build something awesome together! 🚀✨
